[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

I don't know what qualities I should look for when reviewing horror games, but as someone who has been keen on horror games since childhood, I really enjoyed the game.
Jump-scares are unexpected and frightening, but it was the distorted faces and voices in the glitched videos that really struck me as "scary."

As for the points I don't like:
•Acting sucks. There were scenes that I cringed a lot while watching. Even the text messages are cringe... Like, there are literally missing people out there, and yet everyone uses weird emojis in every damn message.
•As someone who loves choice-based games, only a few of your choices affect the ending, and the game has only 4 different endings (which is way less than I expected.)
•I don't want to spoil the endings, but I must say, I didn't like any of them.
•The phone interface is not good. Its functionality is pretty limited. Chatting is slow, you can't switch between tabs; you can't use the tab button on the keyboard to switch between text boxes, and you can't start videos from a certain timestamp.

Other than these, it's definitely a fun and spooky experience. The price is totally acceptable for 5 hours (and multiple playthroughs with a new game+ / fast chatting mode), so I recommend it.

review_text_raw:
My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

This is a decent "choices matter" voyeuristic psychological thriller with the occasional horror elements (jump scares) that is a must play for horror fans and might be worth checking out on sale for people who like story rich games.  Here is what you need to know:
+Doing all interactions through the phone is very well done.
+Phone UI includes a menu of sorts that shows options of things to do next, and choices you have made.
+All character personalities and writing is well done, but...
-Some of the in-person acting via video seems weak, but part of it could be the inherent awkwardness of characters or their situations.
-The story doesn't seem to really branch out, as it seems more on rails than branching given that choices influence actions that contribute to the end result but don't have a notable impact on the story other than how characters react/feel about you.
-Your in-game surroundings/background and the rare background noises outside of the phone have no relevance to what is actually going on, other than to set a "mood" and randomly have the chance at jump scaring you.  IMO all jump scares should happen within the context of what is ACTUALLY happening, otherwise the other jump scares have faster diminishing returns.
?I don't know that I was compelled enough by the story to want to play through again at 3-4 hours length to get a different ending and see how they interact with me differently.

This game's got me heated.

Simulacra is a simulated mobile phone method of delivering a horror game. It is based on the disappearance of a young woman named Anna, and the protagonist (you) has discovered her phone on their doorstep. From there, you delve into the secrets of her phone to find all the information you can, and try to locate--and subsequently save--Anna.

From a mechanical perspective, the game is pretty solid. There's no skeleton or standard out there for "Phone application based horror", making Simulacra a rather noteworthy pioneer and sequel to the developer's predecessor. Applications are sound, mimicking their real-life counterparts exceptionally well. The interface is smooth, and the methods for accessing the different pools of data prove acceptable. My only real complaint is, while the "data restoration" mechanic was easy enough to use, it felt ultimately meaningless and proved only to be a minor time sink. It was an interesting concept, but executed poorly. Perhaps, in later editions, the method for restoring and recovering data might make a more central point in the story.

However, in a game like this, the story is what really holds the fiber and and strength of a game. Hoo boy, does Simulacra tell you a story. The deeper you delve, the closer you get, the more stressful the game will become. Information will consistently surprise the player, and force them to make intensely difficult decisions. While they do have some effect on the ending of the game, the limitation to four significant endings does, to say the least, cause some level of dissonance between decision making and results.

Overall, for five dollars, it was a surprisingly binge-worthy experience.

There's no skeleton or standard out there for "Phone application based horror", making Simulacra a rather noteworthy pioneer and sequel to the developer's predecessor. Applications are sound, mimicking their real-life counterparts exceptionally well. The interface is smooth, and the methods for accessing the different pools of data prove acceptable. My only real complaint is, while the "data restoration" mechanic was easy enough to use, it felt ultimately meaningless and proved only to be a minor time sink. It was an interesting concept, but executed poorly. Perhaps, in later editions, the method for restoring and recovering data might make a more central point in the story. However, in a game like this, the story is what really holds the fiber and and strength of a game. Hoo boy, does Simulacra tell you a story. The deeper you delve, the closer you get, the more stressful the game will become. Information will consistently surprise the player, and force them to make intensely difficult decisions. While they do have some effect on the ending of the game, the limitation to four significant endings does, to say the least, cause some level of dissonance between decision making and results. Overall, for five dollars, it was a surprisingly binge-worthy experience.

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.
- [b]Good Pacing:[/b] The game pushes you in the right direction. If you finish a task, you’ll get an alert letting you know exactly which app or person to investigate next.

[h1]The Not-So-Good[/h1]
- [b]Awkward Acting:[/b] The acting is a little awkward at times. I definitely laughed at a few moments, but it gets the job done and sells the story.

[b]TLDR:[/b] A neat mystery that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens next. If you like unique puzzles and can handle a bit of a creep factor, it’s worth it.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
☐ Skip It
☐ Buy it on Sale
☑️ Worth it at Full Price

A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

[h1]👍 Highly Recommended[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA is one of the few games that genuinely makes browsing through a smartphone feel fun. It's a horror game of sorts, but Instead of running from monsters or hiding in closets, you're piecing together the disappearance of a young woman by exploring every corner of her phone. Messages, photos, videos, emails, social media, and browser history slowly reveal a mystery that's equal parts psychological thriller and supernatural horror. It feels disturbingly believable-almost like scrolling through someone else's real device.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🟢 PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Brilliant Found Phone Concept:[/b] Investigating an entire mystery through a lost smartphone is an incredibly immersive idea that still feels unique years after release.
[*][b]Excellent Storytelling:[/b] The narrative unfolds naturally through text messages, emails, videos, and social media instead of lengthy exposition. Every app contains another piece of the puzzle.
[*][b]Convincing Characters:[/b] Conversations feel surprisingly authentic. Friends, coworkers, and family all have believable personalities and motivations, making the investigation feel personal.
[*][b]Genuinely Creepy:[/b] SIMULACRA builds tension through unsettling discoveries, disturbing videos, and the feeling that something is deeply wrong with the phone itself.
[*][b]Creative Puzzles:[/b] Unlocking files, recovering deleted data, solving passwords, and navigating fake apps keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.
[*][b]Multiple Endings:[/b] Your decisions matter, giving the story additional replay value.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🔴 CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Live-Action Acting Can Be Uneven:[/b] Most performances are convincing, but a handful of scenes feel slightly awkward compared to the otherwise strong production.
[*][b]Occasional Interface Frustrations:[/b] Searching through apps or revisiting conversations can sometimes be more cumbersome than necessary.
[*][b]The Ending May Divide Players:[/b] Without spoilers, the final revelations won't satisfy everyone, especially those hoping for a more grounded explanation.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]💰 VALUE FOR MONEY[/h2]
[b]Excellent[/b] — SIMULACRA offers several hours of engaging investigation packed with memorable moments, clever puzzles, and one of the most original horror concepts in the genre. It's frequently discounted on Steam, making it an even easier recommendation for fans of narrative adventures and psychological horror.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]⭐ 9/10[/h3]
[i]A brilliantly executed smartphone horror that proves the scariest place in a horror game isn't an abandoned mansion. Immersive, unsettling, and remarkably original, SIMULACRA remains one of the most engaging narrative horror experiences available on Steam.[/i]

[disclosure: I got this game for $1 as part of a Humble Bundle. I do think it's worth regular price though.]  

I enjoyed the story and felt they made good use of the mobile interface. It's basically a visual novel, so the story's on rails most of the time. However, there are points where your choices affect your relationships with the other characters, or where you know what to do (get in touch with someone) but not how to do it (you don't know her), so you need to get creative. 

Another nice thing about the game itself is the Begin+ feature, which speeds up the dialogue boxes on subsequent playthroughs. That'll get you through the game in about an hour instead of the usual three or four, making it a bit easier to try other paths and find all of the endings (I'm not there yet.) 

On the downside, I could have done without the pop scares. That's about as cheap as horror gets. Also, since the story and its dialogue options are all laid out for you, sometimes I had to say things I didn't believe or reveal information I wouldn't have revealed, and that hurts the immersion for me. Still, these are minor flaws in a fun, quick, entertaining game.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is essentially a found footage film but as a game.
One day someone leaves you a phone at your doorstep, which belongs to a girl that has gone missing.
From there, it's your job to snoop through her phone to uncover hints on what happened to her.
The actors can be very cheesy and hardly believable, but that has it's own charm if you are into that kind of thing. The problem I had with the story was the horror elements that they try to shove in, in the form of jump scares. Apart from being the annoying type of jump scares, they also immediately take the story in a direction, where you as the player know where the story will end up. If the jump scares where replaced with more subtle hints that something is off, I think it would have been a lot more engaging.
  
To give credit to the devs, they did a good job at imitating a phone OS with  multiple apps. That makes it fun to snoop around for clues on how to gain access to specific parts of the phone. Even though you have a variety of apps to explore, however, multitasking is something that the fake OS lacks, which makes jumping back and forth from different apps a chore. Having to constantly scroll through everything to get to the part you need can quickly become a nuisance, especially when it deletes the things you have to fill in.

Despite these issues, I still enjoyed the game enough to recommend it for the price. It only takes around 3 to 4 hours to finish, but it has multiple endings. A new game plus mode exists, which fast-forwards the conversations. I wish it would skip the puzzles as well, so you can just focus on the endings, but alas, it is what it is.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception.

I am generally biased to be forgiving of FMV interactive movies, so of course I've played others like Her Story, #WarGames, The Bunker, Late Shift, and The Shapeshifting Detective.  Like those games, this game is relatively short on total content, with moments of good acting and then...well, near-miss moments that make you cringe.  Also, these games tend to have multiple achievements and scenes that you can't get in one playthrough, which is a way of extending the replay value, but I seldom feel particularly inclined to watch the repeated parts over and over again.

This game is unique due to the phone interface and the clever design that it took to make that work.  You feel like it really could be you deciding what to do in this situation, but then sometimes you're reminded how you can't actually do anything like answer a phone call.  So when it works, it's great, but it has built-in limitations to just how far the concept can go.  I commend them for the creepy story.  I wish the really uneven voice acting hadn't pulled me out of it from time to time.  At least Anna (whose phone you've found) is done consistently well.

Your first full playthrough will take 3-4 hours depending on how much you read, and subsequent plays should take you a bit less.  Alternate achievements, videos, conversations, and endings are basically earned by the responses you choose, like who to be nice to, who to scold, and who to trust.  The downside of that is like the decisions in Telltale games, especially The Walking Dead: you'll have to replay with lots of choices that you'd never make in real life if you want to see the other paths.  In that regard, replays are more like gaming the game and less like experiencing the story.  But overall, that's a complaint that's bound to be true of every choose-your-own-adventure game you can find.  So you know what you're getting.  If you like that, and you have a tolerance for FMV games, this one is certainly worth $5.

review_text_raw:
A fun, innovative experience involving navigating someone’s digital life to find out what happened to someone.

Background: I like playing interactive stories like this while I’m eating instead of watching TV or a movie. It’s good to play these kinds of games between bites.

I didn’t know what to make of this game—I think I got it as part of a bundle—but installed it and tried it out after running through a few movie games and wanting to shift to something else. I was pleasantly surprised by the story, and the gameplay was similar to games like Her Story and Orwell where you interact with a digital interface to make the story unfold.

The Positives:
-It really does feel like you are a person who found a phone and are trying to find out what happened to the owner. There are a few times where it is imperfect in terms of what you probably could/should/would do, but it does a good enough job that it felt realistic enough to suspend disbelief for several hours.

-The phone was fun to play around with—you go into various apps and learn about the owner’s recent activity and then even get to participate a little.

-The people you interact with are sketchy as hell, but it definitely made things interesting.

-The ending got pretty wild; while the horror elements are minimal for most of the game, the ending combines the genres of tech-thrillers and evil-spirit-horror—very interesting. It’s not simply like System Shock 2 or Terminator (where the tech tries to control you) or Evil Dead or The Ring (where evil spirits are trying to kill you); it’s an interesting mix.

-The people involved did a great job—there are a lot of photos, videos, and conversations, and both the actors and the developers did a great job of making it all fit together. It all felt real—I never thought for a moment that the photos or videos were “fake” or “made-for-the-game”. That’s all I look for in acting; not everything has to be Meryl Streep, and this felt real enough.

-The ending was fresh for me—the combination of it being just slightly different from other endings in the genre along with the uniqueness of me having to make decisions that led to the outcome made the experience very new and interesting.

The Negatives:
-As I mentioned, the people you interact with are sketchy, which I overall enjoyed but it does result in some weird interactions. I thought it worked, but I wouldn’t be surprised if you played and said, “Why don’t they just do X?” — I felt that any plot holes were covered up well enough for me to buy it, but you might not.

-If you like a lot of horror, there isn’t much here—it ratchets up near the end but for the most part is more of a mystery with a dash of spooky/thriller elements. I liked the amount, but you might want more.

-It’s tough to strike a balance between elements that build the character and world with ones that begin to give you hints about the mystery…I think they did a good job, but you might find that early on you go through a lot of videos and photos that don’t reveal much. The photos are easy enough to skim through, but you’ll watch several videos and they don’t really do much other than give you a live look at what the owner looked like while slowly introducing the fact that something is amiss. If you’re a narrative critic, you’d probably want them to have done more with those elements than just a look into the life of the owner.

Overall, it’s an interesting game. I was engaged most of the time and there are only brief periods where there is a lot of text back-and-forth that you might want something more to be happening—but it’s not bad by any means. If you are sucked in at those points, you will enjoy it. If not, that’s probably where you might tune out. The good news is that the developers listened and put in the ability to adjust the speed, etc. of the game (especially if you’re replaying it) to solve for that issue. So I think you’ll be okay. As long as you like the mysterious look-into-the-life-of-someone-else genre of point-and-click games (like the “found footage” genre of movies but for video games), you’ll enjoy it. If you are hoping for a lot of horror, though, there isn’t too much and so I just hope to set your expectations appropriately.

This review may contain light spoilers. The TL;DR is that I would recommend it, it's about 3 hours of gameplay, but is quite hand-holdy in parts. Don't go into this expecting a cerebral game where you need to figure everything out for yourself. Also, don't expect the choices the game forces you into making to make any sense, either.

I quite liked it. It's definitely an improvement from the last game, but there are a few things I noticed.
For instance, there's a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the phone's interface through the game, and most notably the 'BUSTED' chatroom, after it's just 2 people left in it, turns into 'BUSTED' is typing, as if the contact name was called 'BUSTED' and this wasn't actually a chatroom.

The knocking, gasps/breathing 'outside' the phone (This game could also be titled "Millennials don't answer the door simulator 2017") were also unneeded. It wasn't that scary and took away from the game, if you're going I was expecting a jump-scare, or some kind of mechanic where I would need to move around my house to avoid various hostile entities from 'getting me' while I solved the phone mystery. 

It was also a bit too linear and railroady for my tastes. The auto-suggestion mechanic needs a lot more work because I felt like I was constantly being railroaded in the dialogue sections down a path that there's no way I (as a person) would have done or said. I wasn't a fan of the two 'supposed-to-lose' parts, either - I spent a good half an hour on one, hunting around and going into every app and going through every bit of information I had so far trying to get more information. 

The story felt very one-track also. If you compared this game to a visual novel, which is pretty much what this game is, a standard VN player would be very dissapointed with the lack of branching paths, different dialogues, and small amount of endings.

I really want to emphasize that the 'free-roam' hunting for information was the best part of this game, and the dialogue elements forcefeeding you stuff you figured out 10 messages ago was the absolute worst. If the devs want to keep on making games like these, the dialog absolutely needs more work. Additionally it seems like the developers really wanted to characterize these people but in the process of haphazardly sprinkling photographs in there were serious inconsistences. Players are going to be combing through this stuff trying to find precious information and the last thing they need is to be misled due to a mistake.

Overall, though, I recommend a buy if this is the sort of game you like. This is a vast improvement upon the last game and I look forward to this studio's next game.

review_text_raw:
Fun game for something quite different, a bit like a detective style game using a phone interface to get to the truth.

GOOD STUFF: To me, i enjoyed it for the novelty, and there are different endings for your choices.... They have tried some unique puzzle ideas, you do have to go back and forth through lots of phone based media to solve stuff, and the game often gives you options for hints, if you want them, when stuck instead of just straight delivering them to you after 2 seconds.  They tried to capture how the current world of social media and dating can feel and added some light humour throughout the game.  if you like solving crime style puzzles with a little mystery element added on top, it is worth the short playtime for a bit of fun.

BAD STUFF: However the ridiculous immaturity/selfishness/general mood of ALL the characters had me struggling to want to side with, save or even continue to want to interact with almost any of them as the game went on... It almost makes sense, as they are around 20yrs of age, that they would be a little naive, hot headed, horny and impulsive but yeesh.... waaaaay overboard, none of them ever understand if you do anything for the safety of yourself OR them, and so much of the dialogue has an extreme teen gossip feel, omg he said that you said that she did THAAAAT guurrrrrl im not talking for 2 mins to show I hate you!!! :O haha!  
Similarly the options you can choose between often force you to move the game onwards in a way I would never even consider and would actively steer clear of if I was in this situation.... but I understand it's very difficult to set up enough paths for players to feel like they really have a choice with these things.... Still some work could be done to not feeeeeel like your responses are so forced in a certain direction.  Maybe I missed it too at the start? But suggesting your character is unable to speak or something would help make some of the game moments easier to understand/improve immersion as well.

I really appreciate what the devs have done here, and hope they continue to make some fun games with a difference to the standard algorithm stuff that floods the markets these days. It would be great if they can find a way to let characters adapt to understand the players personality and choices a little more, it's so important to games like this where you are expected to solve a crisis situation if it feels even remotely like it was your actual choices as a person that led to the consequences you get :).

This game is fun and I recommend it -- it's a good way to kill a few hours and is a bargain even at full price. The interface is fun, the mystery is fun, the suspense and creepiness is fun. But there are some not-fun things.

* the jumpscares are just kind of pointless. There's no reason for them to exist, not even within the narrative itself. They ended up making me roll my eyes. The Game's scariest moments are the ones where you feel a slow dread due to the knowledge you've gained

* the story isn't thematically coherent. it doesn't know what it's trying to say. in the end it makes some claim about the fakeness of social media or w/e, but that's not really supported by the rest of the game, which spends a lot more time with the cause and effect of non-social media-related interactions. That makes the denouement feel dissatisfying, as a lot of stuff, like the conflict with the ex-boyfriend or the relationship with the best friend, feel like they could have been replaced with anything else and the story remain intact, which means they're just window dressing and not even that important. It feels disrespectful to the player and to the characters.

* the game has multiple endings but doesn't let you skip ahead when dialogue is playing! This is the most irritating oversight. I ended up pulling up Cheat Engine on second playthroughs so I could turn up the game's speed so I didn't have to wait so long for the chat bubbles to show up. 

* dialogue looks like it was written by non-native English speakers, and I don't just mean text speak, I mean grammar wise it's awkward. Could stand to see some copy editing.

* just generally a lot of interesting concepts and ideas that get raised but not carried out to their full potential. There's a lot here to like, but a lot of misses in execution. I liked the interface messing directly with the player that happens partway through the game, but then nothing ever comes of it. It could have been totally cut from the game and the story would remain unchanged, which is just a bummer.

But those are my gripes, I still had a fun time, so yeah, buy the game!

[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

You've obtained the phone of a missing woman named Anna. Your goal is to snoop around her phone's files, social media, and her contacts to get more information about who may have taken her. 

The game simulates what it's like to be in this situation very well with the phone and notification sounds. It feels both dangerous and scandalous at the same time. Like at any moment, police will be knocking on your door asking why you have her phone. 

I actually got a bit invested in figuring out what was going on, but I also wanted to be a terrible person and mislead people to see what would happen. 

Who are you relative to the situation? 
Maybe you're the one who kidnapped her! 
Play the game to see for yourself because I do recommend it.

The main thing dragging back the game isn't the story. It's not the immoral conversations you are having with Anna's abusive ex boyfriend, Greg. It's not even about the advice you're taking from register sex offender, Taylor. 

It's just the cringe acting. 

Honestly that's it. 

The acting is awful, like really acting. Anna sounds like she's reading from a script. Same applies to all characters. From Taylor's singing to Greg cursing you out, these people cannot act.

Another issue is investment in the characters, I don't like any of them so I don't feel for any of them. 

Also the characters are stupid, simply stupid. None of them decide to ever call you out for being a potential suspect, and only one calls the cops after a while.

I'm not a fan of horror genre. I find stupid main characters hard to root for, and just like horror movies on Netflix, I've lowered my expectations to just enjoy the slop.

It's a well put together game, with a believable UI for a Samsung phone.

Yooooo this game is cool!  Simulacra is my first Kaigan game, so if it cribs from any other games they've made, I wouldn't know yet (I've seen reviews saying this game is similar to others, but I'm fresh to the series/catalog..)  

In my first play-through, I failed hard.. Without spoiling too much, let it suffice to say I didn't save the people I was supposed to save.

Some positives:  The choices in the game actually have some bearing on the outcome of the game.  In my first play-through, I chose to be snarky/sarcastic at times.  My snark made me laugh at the time, but came back to bite me in the end.

Still, overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  I found the presentation (playing the entire game via the interface of someone else's phone) to be interesting, and I want to play again and figure out how to get more positive endings than the one I got the first time around.

Went into this completely blind and found it to be a decent game with a slightly above average horror storyline. There are a lot of jump-scare tactics in this visual novel/detective game, many of them unnecessary and overused. The FMVs were done pretty well and the interface is intuitive. The game encourages you to play it again to get different outcomes, but when the first playthrough is over 3 hours I can't be bothered to play a linear story and make sure that I selected certain dialogue options to get all endings/100% achievements.

One thing that I absolutely found hilarious was Greg's voice acting. It's so campy and over-the-top that the first time I heard it I couldn't help but bust out laughing. I'm sure that when he recorded it he had to be clear and precise with his lines, but holy crap it just sounds like a Dragonball Z character powering up for a fight.

I recommend this only because what it does well, it does it *really* well (atmosphere, NPC dialogue, FMV, interface). For the other stuff, it's borderline 80's slasher B-movie status trying to take itself a bit too seriously. There seemed to be some missed opportunities here and gaping plot holes, but I would play another game very similar to this by the same developer with a few new tricks.

Overall, mostly worth your time. Might play Simulacra 2 when I get the chance.

The first playthrough is the most fun because you get to explore the game's limits and be a catfishing detective, although the replay value is pretty low for me because then you realize just how short it really is. For $5 though, it is acceptable. The buildup is great and the ending is decent and not what I expected, but pretty original in its own way. I also think they did a great job with the interface and laid out relatively natural methods for you to do your investigating. The journey was definitely better than the destination for me.

I am a fan of interactive storytelling, but the only thing you really feel invested in is finding out what happened to Anna, and if you're sympathetic, wanting to save her, since she is the only character you really get to know through all your interactions and discoveries. The biggest con for me is that the acting and voice acting was okay at best - at times a little too animated/forced - and I felt if there were more development for the characters, the attachment would truly tear us apart as we are forced to make more choices. Also, the creep factor disappeared for me personally once I got through to the ending.

Overall, I do recommend the game, but not very enthusiastically. It was good, but has a lot of potential to be even better.

Overall a very good game well worth more than its full asking price. Will try again.

A fantastic exercise in intrigue, suspense, horror, social commentary, with well-considered player choice and interactivity. There are a great many wonderful touches to truly immerse you in using a missing person's phone. It's completely diegetic and naturalistic, never straying from the phone's interface. And if you're interested in the idea of desperately looking through someone's phone to find any trace of them, going down a deeper and deeper rabbit hole, you absolutely need to play this game. It is unmatched by any of its peers.

Just keep in mind the production value, so if you're expecting AAA industry level acting from this modest indie studio, remember this is a game made by a small team where you're on a typical phone of an ordinary woman with unremarkable colleagues. Its brilliance lies in the presentation, concept, and suspense. The production flaws and minor mechanical limitations are quick to forgive, and going through again on Begin+ easily makes up for it in my opinion.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10
